newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Nurse's brother awaits Saudi verdicts in anguish.
newsitem.headline: Nurse's brother awaits Saudi verdicts in anguish.

text.p: The brother of an Australian nurse murdered in Saudi Arabia said on Tuesday he had never directly called for the death penalty for two British nurses accused of the killing, although it remained an option.

"We have not ruled out the death penalty but then again we have not ruled it in," Frank Gilford told Reuters in a telephone interview from his home in the small farming town of Jamestown, 120 km (74 miles) north of Adelaide.
"We have never demanded it definitely had to be the death penalty. We have not knocked back our option of exercising our rights (to grant) clemency," Gilford said on Tuesday.
The body of Gilford's sister Yvonne, 55, was discovered in her room at the King Fahd medical complex in the Saudi city of Dhahran in December 1996. She had been stabbed, bludgeoned and suffocated.

Under Saudi law, the victim's immediate family, Frank and his mother Muriel, may demand an execution if the two accused nurses -- Deborah Parry, 41, and Lucille McLaughlan, 31 - are found guilty and the court rules the penalty is appropriate.
Gilford, whose lawyers have previously quoted him as saying the death penalty seemed to be the only right answer in this case, said he had always stated the family would consider all options.
"There is no foregone conclusion that we are going to say 'right, we want their heads chopped off'," Gilford said.
"What we are looking at, is for the court to make a decision and then we can say right, we can look at it," he said.
Asked how he felt with the Saudi court's verdict expected in a few days, Gilford said: "Not very comfortable".
"It is not a situation I would wish on my worst enemy, it is a position I do not feel any person should be put in," he said.
While Saudi law allows a victim's immediate family to demand an execution, the British nurses' lawyers say the family's call must be unanimous.
The nurses' lawyers have launched action in Australia to stop Gilford from calling for the death penalty on his mother's behalf until her mental competence has been determined.

The South Australian state supreme court on Tuesday adjourned until August 26 an application from the nurses to appoint an independent guardian -- the government-appointed public advocate -- to act on Muriel's behalf in the case.
Gilford on Tuesday said he, too, would apply to be appointed guardian and spokesman for his sick mother, but added the move was not designed to bolster his rights in the Saudi case.
"That is not my motivation, my motivation is to look after my family unit," Gilford said.
"All this is doing is to pick on a poor old lady who is 84 and whose only crime is to be old and feeble and to have a daughter who was cruelly murdered," he said.
